A.text: A small vegetable garden needs steady care, but the work changes as the seasons pass. Begin by checking the soil and the condition of the plants. Remove dead leaves, loosen the surface with a hand tool, and add well-rotted organic matter where the ground appears hard or thin. Water the soil when it is dry rather than watering on a fixed routine. Give plants a slow, thorough soak so moisture reaches their roots. Keep the soil slightly damp during warm weather, since frequent shallow watering can leave roots weak. Check it each morning by touching the ground below the surface. Weeds compete with vegetables for moisture and nutrients. Pull them while they are young and before they spread widely. Work carefully around plant stems so their roots are not damaged. A layer of mulch can help by keeping the soil moist, reducing weed growth, and protecting roots from sudden changes in temperature. Use clean garden material and leave some space around each plant so the air can move freely. Watch for leaves with holes, pale patches, sticky surfaces, or curled edges, as these may show that pests are present. Some vegetables need more space than others. Thin crowded seedlings so each can grow well, and decide whether to keep thinnings for transplanting or remove them. Support climbing plants with simple stakes or frames, placing supports before the stems become long and tangled. Pinch off side growth when the plant type benefits from it, and remove damaged leaves that touch the soil. Harvest regularly once vegetables reach a usable size. Frequent picking encourages continued production and prevents fruit from becoming tough or overly mature. As the growing season advances, replenish the soil with compost or another suitable organic feed. Apply it according to the needs of the crop and mix it gently into the surface. Avoid adding too much rich material to leafy vegetables, which can cause excessive leaf growth and weak roots. Rotate the growing area where practical, so the same family of vegetables is not repeatedly planted in the same strip. This can help prevent the buildup of pests and disease. Garden tools should be cleaned after use, especially when they have touched unhealthy plants. During the hottest part of the season, watering may need more attention. Check containers and raised beds often because they dry out faster than open ground. Water in the early or late part of the day, when little heat is lost to evaporation. Direct the water at the base of the plants instead of wetting all the leaves. If leaves wilt in the middle of the day but recover later, the roots may need a deeper watering. Wilting that continues despite moist soil may indicate root trouble, poor drainage, or another problem that requires careful inspection. Protect tender plants from harsh weather. Use cloches, row covers, or a sheltered corner when cold wind or heavy rain is expected. Vent covers during mild daytime periods so warm, damp air does not build up inside. Stake plants that may bend under wind or the weight of their crops. After storms, look for broken stems, flooded soil, and branches that have fallen onto nearby plants. Delay replanting until the ground has drained and the danger of further damage has passed. As the season draws toward its end, plan the remaining harvest. Pick vegetables that are ready and remove plants that have stopped producing. Healthy material can go into a compost heap, while diseased material should be kept away from the growing area. Clear away spent roots and fallen leaves so pests do not have shelter through the colder months. Leave some sound soil structure in place rather than digging heavily. If the soil is compacted, loosen only the upper layer and add organic matter for later. In autumn, plant hardy vegetables suited to cool conditions and protect them from slugs and other pests. Cover the soil with a layer of mulch after the ground has cooled, but keep it away from plant stems. Bare patches of ground can be covered with material that breaks down over time, improving the soil and limiting erosion. Avoid leaving thick wet mulch in place, as it can encourage rot. Check new growth often and replace damaged covers after windy weather. Winter is a time for planning, maintenance, and quiet preparation. Review which vegetables grew well and which suffered from pests or disease. Keep notes on sowing times, spacing, watering needs, and harvest results. Sharpen and clean tools, repair supports, and replace worn parts. Check stored crops and remove any that have spoiled. If compost is available, turn it so it breaks down evenly. Garden structures can be checked for loose joints, but avoid making repairs during wet or icy conditions when working around the plot is uncomfortable or unsafe. As spring returns, prepare the ground without working it while it is saturated. Wait until the soil crumbles rather than sticks together. Add mature compost, remove remaining weeds, and check the condition of covers and supports. Start tender plants in a sheltered, protected space before moving them outside. Harden them gradually by exposing them to outdoor conditions for short periods. Plant outdoors when the soil has warmed and the weather is settled, following the needs of each vegetable. Space plants properly, water them well, and continue checking for pests. This steady, attentive approach helps the garden remain productive through each change of season.

B.text: Bees begin their daily work soon after light appears. Many spend the early part of the morning visiting flowers, collecting nectar and pollen. They move from bloom to bloom, landing on petals and moving their legs over the powdery pollen. A bee carries pollen in special hairs on its body and gathers nectar in its crop. After filling its crop, it may fly back to the hive and give the food to other bees. Some workers clean the empty cells, while others prepare wax, repair the comb or guard the entrance. Bees also regulate the conditions inside the hive. They fan the air with their wings, move water around and feed the young. Their work continues through the day, though heavy rain, strong wind or very cool weather can keep them inside. Ants leave their nest at different times according to the species and the season. Some travel in winding lines along paths they have established over repeated journeys. They follow scents left by other ants and by food along the ground. When one ant finds a useful meal, it often returns to the nest and leaves a trail of scent. Soon others follow the same route. Ants can carry food much larger than themselves, holding it in their jaws while walking or climbing. They may cut pieces from a dead insect, carry seeds or collect honeydew from insects. Their strength comes from the structure of their bodies and from the way their muscles work together. An ant nest is a busy place, although it may look like a simple mound from above. Tunnels connect chambers used for food, eggs, larvae and resting adults. The queen spends much of her life laying eggs. Worker ants feed and clean the larvae, remove waste and repair damaged parts of the nest. When the nest grows crowded or the soil becomes wet, the workers may move eggs and larvae to another site. Ants also take part in wars between colonies. They form groups, use scent to identify nest mates and carry injured workers back inside. Other small insects follow many different daily patterns. Flies may rest on walls, leaves or food during the morning and become active as the day warms. Some feed on decaying material, while others visit flowers, fruit, dung or living animals. Hoverflies hover in the air before landing, and their young may live in decaying plant material beneath the soil. Butterflies often bask in sunlight early in the day, opening their wings to raise their body temperature. Later they sip from flowers or moist ground. Moths usually fly at night and navigate by scent and by faint patterns of light. Dragonflies spend much of the day hunting. They perch on stems, fences or branches and dart out when they see insects moving nearby. Their large eyes help them detect movement in many directions. After catching prey, they often carry it to a perch and eat it there. Ladybirds may feed on plant pests, especially when they wake from a resting period and become hungry. They often remain still for a time, which can make them difficult to notice. Beetles live in many habitats and eat many kinds of material. Some graze on leaves, others on wood, fungi, dung, stored food or small animals. Wood beetles make narrow tunnels in trees and leave small piles of pale fragments behind them. Dung beetles shape pieces of dung into balls and move them away, sometimes burying them in the soil. This helps break down waste and returns material to the ground. Predatory beetles search under stones, beneath loose bark and among fallen leaves. Grasshoppers feed mainly on plants. They often rest low in the grass during the day and become more active when it is cooler. Their strong hind legs allow them to jump away from danger. Caterpillars spend much of the time eating leaves. Their bodies are well suited to clinging to stems, and many of them hide during the brightest hours. When they are ready to change, they may spin a silk pad, hang beneath a leaf or enter the soil. Spiders are not insects, but their everyday habits are closely connected with them. They build webs to catch small flying insects and often repair them throughout the day. Some spiders hide in leaves, crevices or holes and wait without a web. Young spiders may spread out from their nest, while adult females often remain near the same resting place. Small insects also adjust their routines to weather and surroundings. They seek shelter when rain approaches, move into lower areas when the wind is strong and alter their activity when the temperature changes. They use scent, touch, sound and light to find food, nest mates and shelter. Their simple actions, repeated over the day, shape the environment around them. Flowers are pollinated, seeds are moved, soil is turned, pests are eaten and food is carried from place to place. In this quiet way, even the smallest creatures play a large and steady part in the daily life of a garden, a field, a wood or any other patch of land where living things share the surface of the earth.
